title: Address Space
body:
The set of addresses a [[Processes|process]] is allowed to name. Every process gets its
own, and that is the fact that makes processes processes: address `0x4000` in one program
and address `0x4000` in another refer to different physical bytes, so neither can reach the
other's data even by accident.

Two kinds of address, and keeping them apart is the whole of [[Virtual Memory]]:

| | Virtual address | Physical address |
|---|---|---|
| Who uses it | every instruction your program executes | the [[Main memory]] chips |
| Who translates | the MMU, on every access | nobody, it is the real thing |
| Range | the same for every process | one machine-wide set |

## The layout

Inside one address space, the regions from [[Stack and Heap]] and
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]:

```
high  +------------------+
      | stack            |  grows down, one per [[Thread]]
      |        |         |
      |        v         |
      |                  |
      |        ^         |
      |        |         |
      | heap             |  grows up, [[Dynamic Allocation]]
      +------------------+
      | globals / static |  [[Static Allocation]]
      +------------------+
      | code (text)      |  read-only
low   +------------------+
```

The kernel is mapped into every address space too, at addresses the process is not
privileged to touch; that is what [[Supervisor State]] enforces and why reaching the kernel
needs a [[System Call]] rather than a jump.

## Sharing one

[[Thread|Threads]] of a process share the address space; separate processes do not, which
is why they need [[Inter-process Communication]]. [[Shared Memory]] is the deliberate
exception: one region of physical memory mapped into two address spaces at once, so a write
by one is instantly visible to the other, and the [[Critical Section Problem]] becomes
yours.

> **Not to be confused with** COMP 1633's [[Address]], which is the address *of a
> variable*, the thing a [[Pointer]] holds. This note is about the range those addresses
> live in.
